summary: This program uses an ArrayDeque as a double-ended queue to model a browser's history: pages are pushed onto the front as they are visited, going back removes from the front, and trimming old entries removes from the back.

lines.text: Java keywords are case-sensitive, so this must be a lowercase `import` before the file will compile; correct the capital `I` and the program runs as printed. The `Deque` interface is what declares the double-ended queue operations used below.
`ArrayDeque` is the resizable-array implementation of `Deque`, and it is the recommended choice when you need fast additions and removals at both ends.
Declaring the variable as the `Deque` interface while creating an `ArrayDeque` keeps the code tied to the behaviour rather than the implementation, so the concrete class can be swapped later.
`addFirst` pushes a URL onto the front of the deque, which mirrors a browser where the newest page sits at the top of the stack of visited pages.
Because each page was added to the front, this last URL is now the current page and "home" has been pushed all the way to the back.
`forEach` walks the deque from front to back, and the method reference `System.out::println` is shorthand for a lambda that prints each element.

`pollFirst` removes and returns the front element, which is exactly what pressing Back does to the current page. Unlike `removeFirst`, it returns `null` on an empty deque instead of throwing an exception.

lines.code: System.out.println("\nGo back: remove current page (front): " + lastVisited);
lines.text: The `\n` escape sequence inserts a blank line before the text, separating the sections of output visually.
`pollLast` removes from the opposite end, discarding the oldest visited page the way a browser caps how much history it keeps.
Calling `pollLast` a second time trims the next-oldest entry, leaving only the two most recent pages in the deque.
